desc:
In a rectangular grid (0 = free, 1 = blocked) a route goes from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell using steps right and down through free cells only. Two routes are non-touching if they share no cell other than the start and the destination.

Count the unordered pairs of non-touching routes, modulo 1,000,000,007. The start and destination cells are always free, and the grid has at least 2 rows and 2 columns, so two non-touching routes are always different routes.

grid = 2x2 all free              ->  1   (one goes right-down, the other down-right)
grid = 2x3 all free              ->  1
grid = 3x3 all free              ->  3
constraints: grid[0][0] = 0 and the bottom-right cell is 0
hints: Enumerating pairs of routes is hopeless, but two routes can be advanced together: after t steps both are on the anti-diagonal r + c = t.

Two right/down routes that never share a cell cannot cross, so one of them stays strictly above the other on every diagonal. Fix that labelling: it turns unordered pairs into ordered pairs (upper, lower).

State: the diagonal t and the rows (a, b) of the two walkers with a < b. Each walker either goes right or down, giving 4 transitions, and both new cells must be free and keep a' < b'. Count the states that reach the two cells next to the destination.
editorial: Move both routes simultaneously, one step per round. After t steps each route stands on the diagonal r + c = t, so a state is the diagonal together with the two rows (a, b); the columns follow as t - a and t - b. If the routes never share an interior cell they can never swap sides, because a step changes a row by at most one and equal rows on the same diagonal mean the same cell. So for exactly one labelling the 'upper' route (smaller row) stays strictly above the 'lower' one on every interior diagonal; counting only this labelling counts every unordered pair once.

At diagonal 1 the upper route must be at (0, 1) and the lower one at (1, 0). A transition adds 0 or 1 to each row, requires both target cells to lie inside the grid and be free, and requires a' < b'. The routes may finally meet at the destination only: on the last interior diagonal the upper walker must be at (m-2, n-1) and the lower at (m-1, n-2). The answer is the number of ways to reach exactly that state.

There are m + n diagonals and at most min(m, n)<sup>2</sup> states on each, with 4 transitions per state, so the cost is O((m + n) · min(m, n)<sup>2</sup>) time and O(min(m, n)<sup>2</sup>) memory with rolling layers. This is the same non-intersecting-paths idea that the Lindström–Gessel–Viennot lemma generalises.
